clinicalPearls: Caused by the lancet liver fluke Dicrocoelium dendriticum, primarily a parasite of grazing herbivores; human infection is uncommon
The life cycle is unusual, using land snails and then ants as intermediate hosts, with humans infected by accidentally swallowing infected ants on vegetation
Genuine infection may cause right upper quadrant discomfort, dyspepsia, flatulence and, in heavier disease, biliary symptoms
Spurious infection is a well-known trap: eggs appear in stool after eating infected animal liver, without the person actually being parasitised
Diagnosis requires finding characteristic dark operculated eggs in stool, ideally after excluding a liver-containing meal and re-testing on a liver-free diet
Praziquantel is used for treatment, with triclabendazole considered in some settings
Peripheral eosinophilia and mild derangement of liver function tests may be present
reference.pathophysiology: Dicrocoelium dendriticum is a small liver fluke that inhabits the bile ducts of sheep, cattle and other herbivores. Its life cycle is distinctive: eggs passed in faeces are eaten by land snails, larvae are shed in slime balls, and these are consumed by ants, which serve as the second intermediate host. An infected ant is behaviourally altered so that it clings to vegetation and is grazed, allowing the definitive host to ingest the metacercariae. In the rare true human infection, larvae ascend the biliary tree and mature into adults in the intrahepatic bile ducts, where chronic irritation produces ductal inflammation, epithelial hyperplasia and periductal fibrosis analogous to other biliary flukes. More commonly, apparent infection is spurious, reflecting passage of eggs from ingested infected animal liver rather than established parasitism.
additionalDifferentials: Fascioliasis and opisthorchiid liver fluke infection
Spurious egg passage after eating infected liver
Other causes of eosinophilia with hepatobiliary symptoms
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy for the characteristic dark operculated eggs
Repeat stool examination after several days on a liver-free diet to exclude spurious infection
Abdominal ultrasound for biliary changes in symptomatic disease
Duodenal aspirate examination where diagnosis remains uncertain
redFlags: Fever with right upper quadrant pain suggesting cholangitis
Persistent symptoms after treatment prompting reassessment
reference.prognosis: True infection is generally mild and responds to anthelmintic treatment; the main clinical importance is avoiding misdiagnosis, since most positive stools represent harmless spurious egg passage.
pitfalls: Diagnosing genuine infection without excluding spurious egg passage from a recent liver-containing meal
Treating an asymptomatic person on the basis of a single positive stool
Confusing the eggs with those of other liver flukes
Overlooking the ant intermediate host when tracing the source of exposure
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Treat genuine infection with an anthelmintic, using praziquantel, with triclabendazole considered in some settings
Exclude spurious infection by repeating stool examination after several days on a liver-free diet before committing to treatment
Manage biliary and dyspeptic symptoms supportively and reassess after treatment
Confirm cure with follow-up stool microscopy for the characteristic operculated eggs
Advise avoidance of accidental ingestion of ants on vegetation and attention to food hygiene to prevent reinfection
Refer to infectious diseases or tropical medicine where the diagnosis is uncertain or symptoms persist
